extracted.intended_audience: academics, researchers, journal editors, and readers interested in research integrity (especially in mathematics)
extracted.subtask_short: assessing math research papers for publication
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating whether a mathematics research paper meets scholarly publication standards (mathematical correctness, novelty, clarity, and proper editorial/peer-review handling) and deciding on correction or retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum research and mathematical standards
rubrics_metrics.description: “This paper does not meet the minimum research and mathematical standards of Applied Mathematics Letters.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manuscripts must satisfy the journal's baseline expectations for rigor, relevance, and correctness. Failure to meet these standards can justify retraction; the notice attributes publication in this case to an administrative oversight and apologizes to readers that it wasn't detected earlier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical coherence of constructions and arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: “Some of this paper’s constructions and arguments make no sense mathematically.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructions, definitions, proofs, and arguments must be logically coherent and mathematically meaningful. Anti-patterns include gibberish constructions, unsupported manipulations, or statements that lack rigorous justification; such failures are grounds for rejection or retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contains scientific/mathematical content
rubrics_metrics.description: Retraction language referenced elsewhere: paper “contains no scientific content.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A submission must include substantive, nontrivial mathematical content — not merely assertions or vacuous statements. Papers that lack actual results, derivations, or meaningful analysis are inappropriate for scholarly publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty and substantive contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique in the post: “There’s nothing new in this paper… The fact that we haven’t actually added anything to the discussion…”, and author text: “We have not introduced any new hypothesis in this work.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should make clear what is new: new theorems, constructions, proofs, examples, or insights. Claiming importance without adding novelty is an anti-pattern; journals expect papers to advance understanding in some way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper editorial handling and peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Retraction notice: publication was believed to be “the result of an administrative oversight.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals must ensure manuscripts undergo appropriate editorial checks and peer review. Administrative errors or failures in editorial process that allow unsound papers to be published are unacceptable and may lead to retractions and institutional corrective actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Severity-based correction vs. retraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Example retraction contrasted with another notice: one article was retracted, another was “found to contain errors which will be corrected in a revised version to be submitted.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals should assess whether problems are correctable (errata/revision) or fundamental (necessitating retraction). Guidance: minor/errors that can be fixed -> correction/resubmission; fundamental flaws in validity or integrity -> retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate authorship and affiliation information
rubrics_metrics.description: Post notes the author’s email changed between papers and that an author was not actually faculty of the claimed institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should provide truthful, verifiable affiliations and contact details. Editors and publishers should verify authorship and affiliations as part of submission checks; misrepresentation can be a red flag for misconduct or undermine credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility and verifiability
rubrics_metrics.description: Tags and context: the post is filed under categories including “not reproducible” and notes the paper “has not been cited.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Results should be stated and derived so others can check and reproduce arguments or computations. Lack of reproducibility or transparency about derivations undermines acceptance and future citation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and correct use of terminology/hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Commentary: confusion over the word ‘hypothesis’ in mathematics and the paper’s statement “We have not introduced any new hypothesis in this work.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors must use standard mathematical terminology correctly, clearly state assumptions and hypotheses, and define terms. Misuse or ambiguity about hypotheses and assumptions signals poor exposition or misunderstanding and can invalidate conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate venue and seriousness of submission
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion points and comments raise concerns about dubious journals/conferences and prankster-style submissions (e.g., gibberish plenary talks, questionable publishers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should target reputable venues appropriate to the quality and scope of their work. Submissions that appear intentionally frivolous, predatory, or from dubious publishers should be treated skeptically; editors should guard against low-quality or joke submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of logical fallacies and improper defenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Author’s response invoked Einstein and a non sequitur about Nobel Prizes (e.g., “papers rejected by referees and editors have won the NOBEL PRIZE”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defenses of a paper should rely on addressing substantive critiques (pointing to errors, clarifying proofs), not appeals to authority, anecdote, or unrelated claims. Using fallacious reasoning to defend flawed work is an anti-pattern and not a substitute for corrections.
